Introduction Phosphorus (P) rock is a limited resource that is unevenly distributed globally (Daneshgar et al., 2018; Dawson and Hilton, 2011). Current agricultural practices rely on mineral P fertiliser derived from P rock, and its scarcity threatens to cause a food crisis and international conflict (Dawson and Hilton, 2011). Accordingly, the European Union has designated P as a critical raw material. A fraction of the P used as a mineral fertiliser in agriculture reaches the consumer in the form of food, which is subsequently consumed and excreted, eventually ending up in wastewater. P is eliminated from municipal wastewater to minimise high nutrient loads on water bodies. Therefore, sewage sludge has a high P content and may be directly applied as a fertiliser in agriculture (Smil, 2002). However, this P cycling technique carries risks because sewage sludge contains pollutants and pathogens. For these reasons, countries with the highest demand for P rock imports (Daneshgar et al., 2018) are beginning to strengthen P recycling from sewage sludge, which separates beneficial components from harmful ones. Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) in Switzerland and Germany must recover P from sewage sludge beginning in 2026 and 2029, respectively (AbfKlärV, 2017; VVEA, 2015). To meet the upcoming legal regulations, methods for recovering P from sewage sludge must be investigated. Technologies for P recovery depend on the major P-binding forms in sewage sludge, which in turn are determined by the P removal method and sludge treatment process, as well as the raw sewage composition (Yu et al., 2021). Vivianite, Fe3(PO4)2 • 8H2O, has been identified as an important P-binding form in digested sludge from WWTPs that apply chemical P elimination by iron (Fe) precipitants (Wilfert et al., 2016, Wilfert et al., 2018). Chemical release has been explored to recover P from vivianite and magnetic separation has been studied at the pilot scale (ESPP et al., 2021; Prot et al., 2019; Wijdeveld et al., 2022; Wilfert et al., 2019). Nevertheless, further research is required to determine the quantity of vivianite in digested sludge, the variables that control its formation, and how these factors might be altered to promote vivianite formation and recovery. The quantity of vivianite in digested sludge must be determined to better understand its formation and to identify WWTPs with a high potential for recovery. Different vivianite quantification approaches have been proposed, such as sequential extraction, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Mössbauer spectroscopy (Prot et al., 2020; Rothe et al., 2015; Salehin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Wilfert et al., 2018). According to Rothe et al. (2015), approximately 80 % of the P bound in vivianite is released as soluble reactive P by sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH-SRP) based on the scheme published by Psenner et al. (1984), which was slightly modified by Hupfer et al. (1995). However, this P fraction may also contain P other than vivianite. Because vivianite is formed during sludge digestion, an increase in the NaOH-SRP fraction in the digested sludge compared to the activated sludge is suggested as a novel approach to approximate vivianite formation. Using a different sequential extraction method, Wang et al. (2021) extracted 70 % of vivianite references with the solvent 2,2′-bipyridine, a complexing agent for ferrous Fe. XRD detects mineral structures and single reflections increase semi-quantitatively with the amount of mineral in the sample, but they can also vary for other causes (Jian and Hejing, 2003; Madsen et al., 2011). This was the first study to apply, combine and compare these three methods. The factors influencing vivianite formation must be researched to control the process. Vivianite formation in digested sludge has been shown to be dependent on the molar Fe/P ratio (Wilfert et al., 2018). Furthermore, simultaneous formation of vivianite and Fe-sulphides was observed in sewage sludge, indicating competition between the two binding partners for the available Fe (Roussel and Carliell-Marquet, 2016; Wilfert et al., 2016) and, hence, an influence of sulphur (S) on vivianite formation. At the laboratory scale, temperature and alkalinity are of minor importance (Cao et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019) whereas variables such as pH, agitation, organic matter and activity of microorganisms affect vivianite formation (Li and Sheng, 2021; Tian et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019; Zhang, 2012). However, it is yet uncertain whether and which of these variables, in addition to the fundamental dependence on Fe availability, have the greatest influence on the quantity of vivianite generated in operational WWTPs. Therefore, this study applied not only bivariate statistics, to identify the primary controlling parameters, but also multivariate statistics to identify additional significant influencing factors. The investigation of vivianite formation in operational WWTPs ensures that the predictors under consideration are within the suitable scale of municipal wastewater treatment. Increasing the vivianite content in digested sludge could enhance the amount of P that can be recovered as vivianite. When the controlling factors are known, they need to be optimised to promote vivianite formation. fetched_contents.text: Pilot-scale magnetic recovery of vivianite from digested sewage sludge 1. Introduction 1.1. Incentive for recovery Phosphorus (P) is an essential resource for food production and chemical industry. The primary source of phosphorus is phosphate rock. About 80% of mined phosphate rock (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) is used in the fertilizer industry (Van Vuuren et al., 2010). Phosphate rock is a finite resource and reserves are concentrated in a few countries (USGS, 2020). The EU has almost no phosphate rock reserves and depends therefore almost entirely on import from other countries. This means there is a supply risk of phosphorus for the EU. Consequently, this is why the EU added phosphate rock and phosphorus to the list of critical raw materials in 2014 and 2017, respectively (European Commission, 2017, 2014). Hence, phosphorus use has to become more sustainable and should include phosphorus recycling from secondary sources. In 2005, the primary P import of the EU-27 was 1777 kton (van Dijk et al., 2016). Europe's Urban Waste Water Treatment Plants annually remove approximately 370 kton P by immobilization in the sewage sludge (van Dijk et al., 2016). Therefore, about 20% of imported P ends up in sewage sludge, making this a substantial secondary source of P and one of the largest secondary sources after animal manure (Cordell and White, 2013). In 2015, Switzerland implemented legislation demanding P recovery from sewage sludge by 2026, followed by Germany demanding 50% recovery in 2017 (BAFU, 2015; BMUV, 2017). 1.2. Technological gap for decentralized P recovery at iron-dosing WWTPs Land application of sewage sludge is the most straightforward and low-cost option to reuse phosphorus. Besides rising concerns about impurities in sludge such as micropollutants, pathogens, and heavy metals, the biggest challenge with direct land application of sewage sludge is the geographic imbalance of P. There are areas, for example in West-Europe, where there is a P surplus due to manure from livestock farming (MacDonald et al., 2011). Transporting sludge to areas with a P-deficit is economically and environmentally unthinkable due to transport costs and emissions. It is, therefore, desirable to recover a more concentrated phosphorus product. Towards this end, phosphorus can be recovered in a centralized manner by incineration of the sludge followed by chemical leaching of P from the ash. Phosphorus recovery from sludge incineration ash has an advantage due to economy of scale and high recovery efficiency (Korving et al., 2019). However, these technologies rely on expensive and strongly centralized infrastructure. Compliance with phosphorus recovery legislation alone will not be a sufficient reason to build sludge incinerators. Alternatively, phosphorus can be recovered at the wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) by the separation of P-bearing minerals from the sludge, i.e., struvite (Doyle and Parsons, 2002). P-recovery at the WWTP level has been shown to be environmentally more beneficial than sludge incineration, although less phosphorus can be recovered (STOWA, 2016). In municipal wastewater treatment, the most favored advanced phosphorus removal technologies are Chemical Phosphorus Removal (CPR) using iron or aluminum salts and Enhanced Biological Phosphorus Removal (EBPR). EBPR plants have the option to recover a small fraction (10–30%) of the P from the sludge as struvite (MgNH4PO4•6H2O) or calcium phosphate (Egle et al., 2016). For CPR plants, there is currently a technological gap to recover P from the sludge locally at the WWTP. 1.3. Vivianite recovery The majority of WWTP in Europe utilize CPR (Korving et al., 2019). If iron salts are dosed for CPR, phosphorus precipitates as iron phosphate minerals and is immobilized in the produced sludge. This sludge is then often anaerobically digested for hygienisation and energy recovery via methane production. Iron can also be added in the treatment process as a coagulant to enhance primary sedimentation and thus biogas production or to prevent hydrogen sulfide emissions (Charles et al., 2006; Ge et al., 2013). Recently, research has shown that vivianite (Fe3(PO4)2•8(H2O)) is the main iron phosphate mineral that forms during digestion of sewage sludge and that up to 80–90% of all phosphorus in digested sludge can be present as vivianite, provided that enough iron is present (Wilfert, 2018). Unwanted vivianite scaling and accumulation in WWTPs can result in the blockage of pipes which leads to an increased need for maintenance (Prot et al., 2021). The authors also describe simple mitigation strategies (i.e., design and operational considerations) to prevent vivianite scaling. Vivianite is a ferrous iron phosphate mineral with the formula Fe₃(PO₄)₂·8H₂O and is the main iron-phosphate precipitate in digested sludge from wastewater treatment plants that use chemical phosphorus elimination by iron precipitants [N1-F2]. It forms during sludge digestion when sufficient iron is present and is especially abundant in phosphorus-rich sludge because iron salts are commonly dosed for phosphorus removal, causing phosphorus to precipitate as iron phosphate minerals and become immobilized in the sludge [N1-F2]. The evidence also states that vivianite can account for up to 80–90% of phosphorus in digested sludge if enough iron is available, and it is formed during anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge [N5-F1]. This explains why it accumulates in phosphorus-rich sludge: it is a byproduct of iron-driven phosphorus removal and digestion, and it can become concentrated when iron is plentiful.

The magnetic properties that make vivianite recoverable by magnetic separation are paramagnetism and magnetic susceptibility. The evidence directly identifies vivianite as a paramagnetic mineral with a magnetic susceptibility varying from 0.8 to 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ m³/kg [N3-R1][N3-R3]. This means that although vivianite is not strongly magnetic like magnetite, it is still susceptible to magnetic forces and can be separated from non-magnetic material in a magnetic separator. Another source notes that the magnetic force attracting vivianite is proportional to the cube of the particle’s radius, making particle size a dominant factor favoring separation [N3-R2]. This is important because smaller particles may still be recoverable if the magnetic separator is optimized for their size.

The feasibility of separation depends on several conditions. First, the evidence emphasizes that vivianite particles are typically small, ranging from 10 to 200 µm [N5-F1]. Smaller particles can be harder to recover because magnetic separation effectiveness is generally greater for larger particles, and the separation force depends on particle size [N3-R2]. Second, the separation mechanism is supported by pilot-scale evidence: a pilot-scale magnetic separator was used to recover vivianite from digested sewage sludge at a WWTP, with the study describing the use of industrial mining separators designed for paramagnetic minerals [N5-F1][N6-R1]. However, the evidence also notes that vivianite recovery is still a separation challenge because of its small particle size and that lab-scale separation has been demonstrated [N5-F1]. This means the method is feasible in principle, but practical success depends on matching the separator type, field strength, and particle characteristics.

Limitations and conditions under which separation is feasible include the presence of other minerals, sludge composition, and operational parameters. The evidence shows that vivianite can co-occur with Fe-sulphides in sewage sludge, indicating competition between vivianite and sulphide for available Fe [N1-F2]. This suggests that the presence of competing minerals may affect recovery unless preprocessing or operational controls are used to favor vivianite formation. The pilot-scale study also mentions that operational parameters were optimized for vivianite separation [N6-R4], implying that process conditions matter. In addition, the evidence points to the need for preprocessing to prepare the sludge for separation, even though the exact steps are not fully detailed here. Overall, vivianite is recoverable by magnetic separation because it is paramagnetic and can be concentrated, but its recovery is feasible only when the sludge is processed with suitable magnetic equipment and when particle size and competing phases do not overwhelm the separation process [N3-R1][N3-R2][N5-F1].

It fits into broader wastewater sludge recovery and phosphorus recovery strategies as a way to concentrate magnetic or paramagnetic minerals from the sludge matrix and to recover a concentrated phosphorus product without relying on centralized incineration [N5-F1][N5-R1]. The evidence supports lab-scale and pilot-scale recovery, but the method is limited by small particle size, competing minerals, and the need for process optimization [N3-R1][N3-R2][N5-F1][N6-R4]. In practice, it is best understood as part of a decentralized, integrated recovery strategy that complements conventional phosphorus recovery technologies [N4-R1][N5-F1].
